newsitem.title: USA: U.S. disappointed in WTO action on Cuba dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. disappointed in WTO action on Cuba dispute.

text.p: The United States on Thursday challenged the World Trade Organisation's fitness to adjudicate a dispute over U.S. sanctions on Cuba and said it would not cooperate with a WTO investigative panel.

Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, in a statement, expressed U.S. disappointment at the WTO's intervention into its dispute with the European Union over the U.S. Helms-Burton law aimed at stopping foreign investment in Cuba. Eizenstat said Washington would try to settle its differences with the EU directly but would not cooperate with the WTO panel because it does not believe it is fit to review U.S. national security concerns.

"The United States wishes to provide every opportunity to settle our differences with the EU in this dispute," Eizenstat's statement said. "We have been in intense discussions with the EU and agree with the characterisation today by (EU Trade Commissioner) Sir Leon Brittan that we have made 'good progress' regarding the dispute."

Eizenstat added that if no prompt settlement were reached, the United States would formally advise the director-general of the WTO of its view and "we will make clear that the panel established today has no competence to proceed because this is matter of U.S. national security and foreign policy."

A U.S. official told reporters the United States would "go the last mile" to settle the dispute with the EU. But, elaborating on the Eizenstat statement, he said Washington maintains that the issue is a matter of national security and that the WTO has no jurisdiction in the matter.

U.S. officials say the Cuba sanctions policy is legal under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the set of open trading rules that underpins the WTO. Washington cites GATT's Article XXI on "Security Exceptions," which says nothing in the accord should prevent signatories "from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests." EU members and other U.S. trading partners challenge this U.S. interpretation and say Washington's use of the security exception in this case is not legitimate.
